text:
Every day, every day I met her. I confess the truth,
I was glad to meet her, yes, my heart took flight. This year it is two
years ago; now I think of it only when I wish, the whole adventure
amuses and distracts me. And as for the two green bird feathers,
I shall explain that shortly.
We had several places where we could meet, by the mill, on the road,
yes, even in my hut; she came wherever I wished. Good day! she always
called first, and I answered good day.

You are happy today, you are singing, she says, and her eyes sparkle.

Yes, I am happy, I answer. You have a spot there on your shoulder;
it is dust, perhaps it is mud from the road; I want to kiss that spot,
oh, do let me kiss it. Everything about you affects me tenderly,
I am so distraught over you. Last night I did not sleep.

And it was true; for more than one night I lay sleepless.

We walk side by side along the road.

What do you think, am I behaving as you like? she says. Perhaps
I talk too much? No? Yes, but you must tell me what you think.
Sometimes I think to myself that this can never turn out well....

What is it that will not turn out well? I ask.

This thing between us. That it will not turn out well. Whether you
believe it or not, I am walking here shivering now; a chill runs
down my back merely when I come near you. It is from happiness.

Yes, the same with me, I answer; a chill also runs through me merely
when I see you. Oh, it will surely turn out well. Besides, I shall pat
you a little on the back to warm you.

She reluctantly lets me do it; I pat a little harder, only in jest;
I laugh and ask whether it does not help.

Oh no, do not be so kind as to thump me on the back anymore, she says.

Those few words! It sounded so helpless to me when she said:
do not be so kind.

Then we went on along the road. Is she displeased with me because
of my jest? I asked myself, and I thought: let us see.
I said:

I happen to remember something. Once, on a sleigh ride, there was
a young lady who took a white silk handkerchief from around her own neck
and tied it around mine. In the evening I said to the lady: You shall
have Your handkerchief back tomorrow; I shall have it washed. No,
she answered, let me have it now; I want to keep it as it is,
just as You have worn it. And she was given the handkerchief. Three years
later I met the young lady again. The handkerchief? I said. She
brought the handkerchief. It lay in its paper, still unwashed; I saw it myself.

Edvarda glanced up at me.

Yes? What happened then?

No, there was no more, I said. But I thought it was a
lovely gesture.

Pause.

Where is that lady now?

Abroad.

23 — Hamsun: II
We spoke no more about it. But when she was going home, she said:

Good night, then. Do not go on thinking about that lady, will you?
I think of no one but you.

I believed her; I saw that she meant what she said, and it was enough
for me for all eternity if only she thought of me. I followed her.

Thank you, Edvarda, I said. Later I added with all my heart: You
are far too good for me, but I am grateful that you want me;
God will reward you for it. I may not be as splendid as
many others you could have; but I am so entirely yours, so violently
yours, by my immortal soul. What are you thinking about? There are
tears in your eyes.

It was nothing, she answered. It sounded so strange that
God would reward me for it. You say such things as.... I
love you so much!

She suddenly threw her arms around my neck right in the middle of the road
and kissed me passionately.

When she had gone, I turned aside and slipped into the forest to hide
and be alone with my joy. And, deeply moved, I ran back
to the road again and looked to see whether anyone might have noticed that
I went in there. But I saw no one.

XIII

Summer nights and still water and endlessly still forests. No
cry, no footstep from the roads; my heart was full as though with
dark wine.

Moths and hawk moths come flying soundlessly in through my
window, lured here by the glow from the hearth and by the smell of my
roasted bird. They strike the ceiling with a dull sound, whir
past my ears so that a chill passes through me, and settle
on my white powder horn on the wall. I observe them; they sit
trembling and look at me; they are spinners, borers, and moths. I
think some of them are like flying pansies.

I step outside the hut and listen. Nothing, no mountain farm,
everything sleeps. The air glows with flying insects, with myriads of
whirring wings. Over at the edge of the forest stand ferns and monkshood;
the bearberry is in bloom, and I love its little flowers. Thank
You, my God, for every heather blossom I have seen; they have been like little
roses on my path, and I weep for love of them. Somewhere
nearby there are wild pinks; I do not see them, but I
sense their fragrance.

But now, in the hours of night, great white flowers have suddenly
unfolded in the forest; their stigmas stand open, they breathe. And shaggy
hawk moths descend into their petals and make the whole
plant tremble. I go from one flower to another;
they are intoxicated, they are sexually intoxicated flowers, and I see
how they become intoxicated.

Light footsteps, a human being’s breath, a cheerful good evening.

I answer and throw myself down on the road and embrace the two knees
and the poor dress.

Good evening, Edvarda! I say once again, exhausted with happiness.

How you love me! she whispers.

How grateful I can be! I answer. You are mine, and
all day my heart lies still within me and thinks of you. You
are the most beautiful girl on this earth, and I have kissed you.
Often I blush with joy merely when I remember that I have
kissed you.

Why have you come to love me so much this very evening? she asks.

And I had for countless reasons; I had only needed
to think of her for it to happen. That gaze beneath the arched eyebrows
high upon her forehead, and that dark, lovely skin!

Should I not love you! I say. I go about thanking
every tree because you are well and in good health. Once, at a ball,
there was a young lady who sat out dance after dance, and everyone left
her sitting. I did not know her, but her face made
an impression on me, and I bowed to her. Well? No, she shook
her head. Does the young lady not dance? I said. Can You understand it,
she answered; my father was so handsome and my mother was a perfect
beauty, and my father swept my mother off her feet. But I
became lame.

Edvarda looked at me.

Let us sit down, she said.

We sat down in the heather.

Do you know what my friend says about you? she began. You
have the eyes of an animal, she says, and when you look at her you drive her
mad. It is as though you were touching her, she says.
